comments.text:
NETWORK CONFIRMED 2026-07-30: phase 1 runs on the existing MAINNET solomint. A signet federation was
considered and rejected. Recording the reason, because it is non-obvious and will otherwise be
re-proposed — free test coins are an obviously attractive idea and the blocker is two steps away.

## Why signet does not work for THIS run
A federation alone cannot sell anything. lnrent's lnv2 receive path mints its bolt11 by doing a
GATEWAY round-trip (fedimint's `create_contract_and_fetch_invoice` fetches the invoice from an
lnv2-capable gateway), so with no gateway attached there is no payable invoice — no order, no
settlement, no lifecycle to observe. A gateway-less fed is not a cheaper phase 1; it is a phase 1 that
cannot start.

And the existing gateway CANNOT serve a signet fed: gatewayd and the fenix lnd in
`ostracoda-lnd-node` are mainnet, so a signet fed is a network mismatch it will refuse to register
with.

So "deploy a signet fed" is really a four-component build:
  1. signet chain access (an esplora URL, or a signet bitcoind — the cluster has only mainnet,
     ns bitcoind, RPC :8332 with a mainnet UTXO snapshot)
  2. a signet Lightning node — none exists
  3. a signet gatewayd — none exists
  4. the signet solomint itself
plus signet channels with INBOUND liquidity before it can receive at all, which on bare signet means
sourcing peers and coins by hand. (Mutinynet would be the better target if this is ever revisited: a
faucet and 30-second blocks, which matter a lot when deliberately compressing periods to hours.)

## What mainnet costs here, for the record
Small and already accounted for in this bead's decisions: a fresh wallet, ~125 sat per 3h
subscription at the proportionally scaled price, a few thousand sat total across several
subscriptions plus renewals. The federation is `solomint` (NOT `solomint-iroh`) — the one lnrent-7qc
vetted, with the ostracoda gateway passing preflight.

Both are mainnet: verified `FM_BITCOIN_NETWORK=bitcoin` and bitcoind RPC :8332 on each deployment
(signet would be :38332).

## If a free-coins environment IS wanted later
File it as its own bead covering all four components — phases 1-4 would all benefit, so the setup cost
amortises. Do NOT bolt it onto a dogfood bead: it is infra with its own liquidity problem, and
discovering that mid-run is how a run gets abandoned half-finished. Nothing was deployed while this was
explored; the devops repo is untouched.

title: PHASE 2 dogfood: the same do-vps lifecycle on phoenixd, after tof's acceptance matrix
description:
## Outcome
PHASE 2 of the operator's phased programme: the same do-vps lifecycle dogfood as lnrent-9q9, run on
`payment_backend=phoenixd` instead of fedimint — several concurrent subscriptions carried through
renew, cancel, expire, suspend and destroy against the live mainnet phoenixd node.

## Why this is separate from lnrent-tof, and strictly after it
lnrent-tof is the ACCEPTANCE MATRIX: does each phoenixd scenario behave correctly (golden path,
refund through LN-address and LNURL, restart during settlement and during a refund, the doctor
positive/negative matrix, reconcile vs getbalance, backup and clean-room restore). It answers "is
this backend correct".

This bead is the DOGFOOD: live with it, over time, with several subscriptions whose deadlines
actually arrive. It answers "does an operator's month on phoenixd work". tof must pass first —
putting a month of real money through a backend whose failure matrix has not been run is the wrong
order, and tof is also where the phoenixd runbook (lnrent-5ik) gets executed and proven.

## What phase 2 adds over phase 1
The economics differ sharply on phoenixd and only show up over a lifecycle:
- The FIRST receive is nearly all fee (measured 2026-07-26: 25,000 sat in, `receivedSat` 2723 — an
  ~89% haircut to ACINQ's first-channel open). Renewals after that are cheap. A multi-subscription
  run is the first time the shape of that curve is visible to an operator.
- Refunds are capped at the NET wallet credit (ADR-0019), so an early-lifecycle refund on phoenixd
  returns a small fraction. Phase 1 on fedimint has a much gentler version of the same effect.
- Fee credit is counted by `receivedSat` and is NOT spendable, with no per-receipt attribution, so
  `spendable_credit_msat` can refuse to book a receipt an unfunded wallet cannot back. That refusal
  is expected on a fresh node's first small sale and is exactly what lnrent-gc7 alerts on.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The same six reconcile arms as lnrent-9q9, observed or explicitly not-reached, on phoenixd.
- The first-receive haircut and at least one renewal receive recorded with real figures, so
  lnrent-ohd's economics doc is written from a lifecycle rather than a single measurement.
- Any fee-credit refusal encountered is recorded with what the operator saw and how they recovered.
- Wallet, seed location and closing balance recorded per lnrent-rwv.
- Docs or operator surfaces that misled are filed as their own beads.

title: PHASE 3: multi-recipe serving — one daemon sells several services (the capability, not recipe depth)
description:
## Outcome
PHASE 3: ONE daemon sells SEVERAL services. This is the capability an Operator needs to have a
product line at all, and it is the point of the phase — NOT the depth of any one recipe. Recipe
deepness (a production-grade WireGuard peer, hardened hosts) is phase 5.

## Where it stands today
The daemon serves exactly one recipe. `daemon/src/main.rs:622-630` collects every valid recipe, sorts
them by service id, takes `.next()`, and warns "M1a serves a single recipe; ignoring the rest". Drop a
second recipe in `recipes/` today and it is silently ignored (alphabetically `do-vps` wins).

But the DATA MODEL already anticipates several:
- `store.rs:100` — "listings are their own table (one recipe -> many)"
- subscriptions carry `recipe_id`
- lnrent-yjl (CLOSED) gated the destructive reconcile arms on it, because "one recipe's provisioner
  must never run its destroy against" another's (provision.rs:653)
- lnrent-6id is the REMAINING ungated arm

So this is a serving-layer feature over a money core that was built expecting it.

## Prove it with recipes that already work — no new recipe needed
`recipes/do-vps` and `recipes/dummy` are BOTH fully functional today (dummy: zero stubs across
provision/destroy/suspend/resume/healthcheck, 100 sat, instant echo-creds). Two real services, two
price points, two provisioning shapes — enough to prove the capability without writing a line of
recipe code.

`recipes/wireguard` is a stub in every hook and stays out of this phase; a real second SERVICE is
phase 4, which becomes cheap once this capability exists.

## lnrent-6id is MANDATORY here, not optional
`fire_soft_reminder` mints the renewal invoice at the SERVED recipe's `pricing.amount_sat` rather than
the subscription's own. Single-recipe it cannot fire. The moment one daemon serves two recipes at
different prices — do-vps at 30000 and dummy at 100 — it is a live wrong-price renewal on real money.
It must land before or with this phase.

## What to build
- Load and serve ALL valid recipes rather than the first.
- A listing per recipe (the schema already supports it).
- Per-recipe `listing publish` / `listing withdraw`. The lnrent-i23 verbs currently resolve
  `recipes.first()` (e.g. ipc.rs:1195), so they need a recipe selector and `lnrent status` needs to
  report several listings rather than one.
- Order intake routes by `listing_id` to the owning recipe — it already loads the listing and checks
  `recipe_id`, so verify rather than assume.
- Every reconcile arm gated on `recipe_id` (yjl did the destructive ones; 6id is the rest).
- `lnrent preflight` runs per recipe and reports which one each failure belongs to.

## Design questions to SETTLE IN THE TASK FILE before draining
Leaving these open is how a reviewer panel churns:
1. One operator identity publishing several 30402s, or an identity per service? (One identity is
   simpler and matches CONTEXT.md's "One Operator has a single brand"; confirm against §5.4's
   coordinate `30402:<pubkey>:<d>` — `d` is the recipe id, so one identity already works.)
2. Does the host capacity budget SPAN recipes or partition per recipe? A shared budget means one
   service can starve another; per-recipe means unused capacity is stranded.
3. What does `lnrent money`'s refund-liability coverage mean across recipes — one pooled wallet
   backing all services, or per-recipe accounting? (The wallet is one; say so explicitly.)

## Acceptance Criteria
- One daemon serves do-vps AND dummy, each with its own published listing, and a Buyer can order
  either and get the right service at the right price.
- A renewal on each charges THAT subscription's price (the 6id regression, pinned by a test).
- Publish/withdraw work per recipe; withdrawing one leaves the other selling.
- The full lifecycle from lnrent-9q9 runs on both concurrently, on compressed periods, real sats.
- The three design questions above are answered in code comments where the next reader will look.

comments.author: master
comments.text:
DESIGN QUESTIONS SETTLED 2026-07-29/30 in a design interview. Two were answered; one dissolved.

## Q1 — one operator identity, or one per service? SETTLED BY CONSTRUCTION, no work needed.
`d_tag(recipe)` IS `recipe.service.id` (daemon/src/listing.rs:257-259), so the coordinate is
`30402:<operator>:<recipe-id>` (listing.rs:263-265). NIP-99 addressable replaceables are keyed on
`(kind, pubkey, d)`, so ONE operator key already yields a distinct listing per recipe — three recipes
are three listings under one identity with no change at all. It also matches CONTEXT.md's "One
Operator has a single brand (Master identity)". There was never a choice here; do not spend a task
file paragraph on it.

## Q2 — shared capacity pool or per-recipe slices? BOTH.
The pool is PHYSICAL TRUTH and is always enforced: `box.capacity_json` parsed into a `Budget`
(supervisor.rs `parse_budget`), with the small bounded `M1A_FALLBACK_BUDGET` when no box row exists.
One host has one CPU count, and a per-recipe slice promising more than the box can run would be a lie
the reservation system would happily tell.

An OPTIONAL per-recipe cap sits on top as operator POLICY, to stop one service eating the box out
from under another. Both are checked; an order must fit the pool AND (if set) its recipe's cap.

The property that makes this better than either pure option:
**CAPS MAY SUM TO MORE THAN THE POOL.** They are CEILINGS, not allocations. So an operator can say
"at most 4 droplets and at most 20 relays" on a box that cannot host both maxima, and get starvation
protection WITHOUT stranding idle capacity the way true slices do. The pool rejects whatever does not
physically fit, so a cap can never over-promise.

Unset cap == no cap, i.e. exactly today's pure-pool behaviour. That must remain the default so this
feature cannot change the semantics of an existing single-recipe install.

### IMPLEMENTATION TRAP — the cap needs `recipe_id` ON THE RESERVATION ROW
Do not compute per-recipe usage by joining `reservation` to `subscription`. It would silently
undercount:
- `reservation` (store.rs:153) has no `recipe_id` — only `order_id`, resources, ports, state, expiry.
- Capacity is reserved at order-intake STEP 3 (order_intake.rs:179) while the subscription row is
  written at STEP 5 (order_intake.rs:256), inside the commit transaction.
- So for the whole `create_invoice` window — a network round-trip, the widest gap in intake — a HELD
  hold has NO subscription row to join to. A join-based per-recipe usage query would miss exactly the
  in-flight holds the cap exists to bound, and the cap could be exceeded.

So: carry `recipe_id` on the reservation row (migration + set it at reserve time), and scope the
per-recipe usage query to it. The existing pool check (`live_usage` excluding this order's own hold,
reservation.rs:143-149) is the pattern to mirror — including the exclude-self behaviour, or a HELD
retry on a capped recipe will reject itself.

## Q3 — refund-liability coverage across recipes. ONE WALLET, say so explicitly.
There is one backend wallet per daemon; it backs every service that daemon sells. `lnrent money`'s
coverage answer is therefore ALREADY pooled and correct as-is — no per-recipe accounting. What the
task file must do is state it, because an operator reading a per-service listing view could
reasonably assume per-service funds.

## Reporting requirement that removes the main reason to want slices
Even under a shared pool, `lnrent status` / `lnrent money` MUST attribute live capacity per recipe, so
an operator who is full can see WHICH service ate the box. That is reporting, not accounting, and it
is cheap — and it is the actual need behind most requests for hard slices.

comments.author: master
comments.text:
CAP SHAPE SETTLED 2026-07-30, correcting sloppy language in the previous comment.

## The cap is a CONCURRENCY limit on live Instances — NOT a lifetime sales count
An earlier note described it as "this service is meant to be sold at most N times". That is wrong and
means something quite different: a lifetime sales cap would retire a service permanently after N
orders. What is wanted is a limit on how many are RUNNING AT ONCE.

CONTEXT.md is precise about the term: an **Instance** is "the actual provisioned resource lnrent
manages", and "One Subscription -> one Instance (v1)". So the knob is:

    at most N concurrently-live Instances of recipe R

## Why this is simpler than what the previous comment implied
It is a COUNT, not a resource quantity. Per-instance resource cost is already declared in
`recipe.toml`'s `resources = { cpu, mem_mb, disk_gb }`, and the physical pool
(`box.capacity_json`) already bounds the total of those. The cap adds one orthogonal thing —
how many of this service may exist simultaneously — so it needs no per-recipe cpu/mem/disk
arithmetic at all.

It also matches how capacity is already enforced: `live_usage` (reservation.rs) counts LIVE holds and
deliberately excludes historical ones. The cap is the same question asked per recipe: count live, not
ever-sold.

## What "live" must mean, precisely
Count both live reservations AND active instances, i.e. the same population the pool counts:
- a HELD reservation (an order mid-flight, before its Instance exists)
- a CONSUMED reservation (the active Instance's capacity hold — reservation.rs's `consume` makes
  CONSUMED the live Instance's hold)
and NOT: RELEASED holds, terminated subscriptions, or anything historical.

Excluding HELD would let the cap be blown through by concurrent orders during the `create_invoice`
window — the same hole the recipe_id-on-the-reservation-row note in the previous comment exists to
close. The two are the same requirement seen from different sides.

## Where it lives — OPERATOR CONFIG, not recipe.toml (decided)
A cap is a property of THIS operator's box and business, not of the service. The same wireguard recipe
should sell 50 peers on a large host and 5 on a small one; putting the number in `recipe.toml` would
let the recipe author decide the operator's capacity and would mean editing a shared recipe to change
local policy.

Two precedents in the tree point the same way: lnrent-o4k dropped a config field that was required at
bootstrap but ignored by the backend, and ADR-0007 forbids a recipe claiming a `tier` above what the
host actually guarantees. Recipes describe the SERVICE; the operator describes their MACHINE.
`resources` is intrinsic to the service (its cost); a cap is not (its limit).

Cost to acknowledge: store.rs:32 records a deliberate stance of "a single operator-tunable knob: one
named const, no per-table/config policy engine". This adds config surface to something kept
deliberately thin — say so in the task file rather than meeting it as a review objection.

comments.author: master
comments.text:
BUYER-FACING ANSWER SETTLED 2026-07-30: a per-recipe cap hit reuses `CapacityFull`. No new wire code.

## Why deliberately the same code
1. Distinguishing them LEAKS OPERATOR POLICY to strangers. "I have room and will not sell you this"
   tells a Buyer — including a hostile one — the shape of the operator's capacity and intent.
   `CapacityFull` reveals only "not selling right now", which is all a Buyer needs.
2. It would be a WIRE CHANGE. `wire/src/dm.rs` fixes the `order.error` vocabulary, so a new code means
   clients that do not know it fall back to generic handling anyway — the benefit only lands once
   clients are updated, a poor trade for a phase-3 feature.
3. The Buyer's CORRECT ACTION IS IDENTICAL either way: this listing is not selling, so look at the
   operator's other listings, which are discoverable from the same 30402 set under the same pubkey
   (one identity, one listing per recipe — see the Q1 note). They do not need the reason to act right.

Order intake already treats `CapacityFull` as "a normal business result", so nothing changes there.

## The condition that makes this defensible — NOT optional
The operator MUST be able to tell them apart even though the Buyer cannot. Without that, a service
silently stops selling on a box with free capacity and there is no way to diagnose why.

So `lnrent status` (and `lnrent money`'s capacity view) must distinguish:
- POOL FULL — the box is out of cpu/mem/disk/ports
- CAP HIT for recipe R — the box has room, but R is at its configured live-Instance limit

This is what promotes the per-recipe attribution requirement from the Q2 note out of "nice reporting"
and into load-bearing: it is the ONLY place the distinction exists. If the reporting is skipped, this
decision becomes indefensible and the wire code would have to be added after all.

comments.author: master
comments.text:
PREFLIGHT SCOPING SETTLED 2026-07-30: a structural failure in one recipe blocks ONLY that recipe's
listing. Per-recipe isolation.

## Why isolation, not daemon-wide
A structural failure is the class lnrent-i23 hard-blocks with NO override. Daemon-wide scoping would
mean a typo in a service not yet being sold takes the LIVE services offline at their next publish —
the same shape of false dependency as blocking phase 1 behind rwv. An operator with three products
must be able to fix one while the other two keep selling.

## The load path already behaves correctly — inherit it, do not reinvent
`load_operator_recipe` (daemon/src/main.rs:608-620) validates each recipe INDEPENDENTLY, logs
"recipe failed validation — DISABLED" per recipe, and only fails when NONE validate. So one broken
recipe already cannot take down the others at load time. Multi-recipe serving gets that for free; the
gap is only at publish/preflight time.

## The checks split two ways — this is the implementable part
Today's five checks (daemon/src/preflight.rs) classify cleanly:

SHARED — one wallet backs every service, so a failure here really does affect all recipes:
  - `gateway`      (:274) refund gateway reachability
  - `federation`   (:312) guardians
  - `lnv2`         (:347) the lnv2 money path
  (and the phoenixd probe on that backend)

PER-RECIPE — a failure belongs to exactly one recipe and must block only its listing:
  - `provider_token`   (:573) — ALREADY per-recipe in spirit: it skips entirely when no loaded recipe
                       declares DO_TOKEN, and an absent token for a recipe that DOES declare it is
                       `fail_structural`. So a host-backend recipe like wireguard/dummy is unaffected
                       by a missing DO token that blocks do-vps.
  - `recipe_preflight` (:643) — lnrent-1sr's provisioning-param validation, inherently per-recipe.

So the machinery partly exists: the skip/NotApplicable pattern is already the right shape. What is
MISSING is ATTRIBUTION — each check needs to carry which recipe it belongs to (or none, for shared),
so `publish` for recipe R gates on R's checks plus the shared ones and ignores the rest.

`lnrent preflight` should keep showing everything, grouped by recipe, since the operator wants the
whole picture; only the PUBLISH gate filters.

## Acceptance note for this bead
A broken `do-vps` region slug must leave `dummy` publishable, and `lnrent preflight` must make clear
which recipe each failure belongs to — otherwise an operator sees a structural failure and cannot tell
which of their three products it blocks.

comments.author: master
comments.text:
TWO CORRECTIONS 2026-07-30 from a two-model review of this bead's own decisions.

## 1. A citation in this thread conflates two different axes — do not inherit it
An earlier comment cites `store.rs:100` ("listings are their own table (one recipe -> many)") as
evidence that "the data model already anticipates several" RECIPES. It does not. That comment
anticipates several LISTINGS PER ONE RECIPE — a different axis, and one this bead does NOT build: this
bead builds a listing PER recipe.

Worse, many-listings-per-recipe is not implemented at all: `listing::d_tag` IS `recipe.service.id`
(daemon/src/listing.rs:255-259), so the coordinate `30402:<operator>:<recipe-id>` structurally forces
ONE listing per recipe. CONTEXT.md:94/:99 and its example dialogue at :214-218 overstate it as working;
that is now filed as lnrent-lwv.

The REAL evidence for this bead's premise is what the same comment also cites and should have led with:
`subscription.recipe_id`, the lnrent-yjl gates on it, and provision.rs:653's warning that one recipe's
provisioner must never run its destroy against another's. Those are per-RECIPE and they do show the
money core was built expecting several.

## 2. The CapacityFull decision is right, but one of its three arguments is weak
Argument (1) was "distinguishing a cap hit from a full pool leaks operator policy to strangers". That
is thin: `capacity_full` already tells a Buyer "not selling right now", and a Buyer can probe the
operator's other listings regardless — the marginal information leaked by a distinct code is small.

The decision stands on arguments (2) and (3), which are sound on their own: it is a wire change against
`wire/src/dm.rs`'s fixed `order.error` vocabulary that only pays off once clients update, and the
Buyer's correct action is identical either way. Do not rely on the leak argument when defending this
choice; it will not survive scrutiny and it is not needed.

ADDITIONAL ACCEPTANCE ITEM from the review: pin a test that a cap hit emits `capacity_full` on the wire,
so a later refactor cannot quietly invent a new code and reopen a settled question.

## 3. One consequence to state in the task file
Counting the same population as the pool (HELD + CONSUMED) means a SUSPENDED subscription still holds a
cap slot — its reservation is deliberately kept per SPEC §9.3:1116-1118. That is defensible (its disk is
still held) but it IS a policy consequence: an operator at their cap with several suspended-but-not-yet-
destroyed subs cannot sell more of that service until retention elapses. Say so, so it is a choice
rather than a surprise.

title: PHASE 4: a third service, a Nostr relay, from the same daemon — proves multi-recipe generalises
description:
## Outcome
PHASE 4: a THIRD service, and a genuinely different one — a Nostr relay — sold from the SAME daemon
that already sells do-vps and dummy. Once lnrent-ja2's multi-recipe capability exists this is
mostly recipe authoring, which is the point: the second service proves the capability, the third
proves the capability GENERALISES.

## Why a relay is the right third service
It is unlike both existing recipes in ways that stress different parts of the seam:
- It is a LONG-LIVED daemon the operator hosts, not an instant credential (dummy) and not a
  provider-API droplet (do-vps). suspend/resume mean actually stopping and starting a process.
- Delivery is an ENDPOINT (a wss:// URL the Buyer configures clients against), not credentials and
  not a config file — a third delivery shape.
- It has real per-tenant state (the relay's event store) that destroy must actually remove, so the
  teardown path has something to get wrong.
- It is self-referential in a useful way: lnrent's own money DMs ride Nostr relays, so the operator
  ends up understanding relay behaviour from both sides — which is exactly the knowledge gap
  lnrent-2em's relay-selection acceptance note calls out.

`recipes/` currently holds do-vps, dummy and the all-stub wireguard. SPEC.md §14 lists `vm/`,
`hermes/` and `fedimint/` as planned recipes; a relay is not yet among them, so this phase adds one.

## What "introduce a service" costs once ja2 lands
Authoring a recipe means: `recipe.toml` (service metadata, pricing, params, declared operations) plus
the hooks — provision, destroy, suspend, resume, healthcheck, and any `ops/`. The wireguard stub is
the shape to follow; do-vps is the only worked example of a real one.

This phase is therefore ALSO the honest test of whether a third party could author a recipe from the
docs alone. Record every place the recipe-authoring path was guesswork — that finding is worth more
than the relay itself, because CONTEXT.md's thesis is an ecosystem of operators, and operators will
want their own services.

## Deliberately NOT here
- Recipe DEPTH and hardening — phase 5.
- Multi-recipe serving itself — lnrent-ja2, which this depends on.
- Choosing the relay implementation is left open on purpose (strfry, nostr-rs-relay, …); pick at
  authoring time and record why, since resource shape and per-tenant isolation differ between them.

## Acceptance Criteria
- One daemon sells three services concurrently, each with its own listing and price.
- A Buyer orders the relay, receives a working endpoint, and can actually publish and read an event
  through it.
- suspend stops the relay and resume restarts it, without losing the tenant's stored events;
  destroy removes both the process and its data.
- The full lifecycle from lnrent-9q9 runs against it on compressed periods, real sats.
- Every gap in the recipe-authoring documentation is filed as its own bead.

title: CONTEXT.md lacks the terms the roadmap turns on (launch/go-live/dogfood, pool vs cap), and overstates many-Listings-per-Recipe
description:
## Outcome
`CONTEXT.md` gains the terms the roadmap actually turns on, and its one wrong-in-a-dangerous-direction
entry is flagged for whoever closes lnrent-kr1.

## Why this is not pedantry — an undefined term minted a phantom gate
`CONTEXT.md` defines neither "launch" nor "go-live". Because no definition existed, a second-model
audit wrote "nothing operator-facing launches before this closes" into lnrent-ehu's description on
2026-07-17, and that unratified sentence — present in no ADR and no SPEC section — became the strictest
rule on master and inverted the P1 frontier for twelve days, while docs/go-live.md:31 simultaneously
said the fedimint path was "go-live-ready" in the present tense. The structural fix is a definition, so
the next audit cannot mint the same phantom.

The interview that found this also stumbled on "sold N times" vs "N concurrently-live Instances" — two
different knobs, and exactly the failure a glossary exists to prevent.

## Terms to add
Keep it a GLOSSARY: what each term MEANS, in observable and implementation-neutral language. Eligibility
criteria, procedures and readiness claims belong in SPEC / go-live.md / the beads, NOT here.

- **Dogfood** — the author operating their own service for real money to learn how it behaves; the
  phases on lnrent-9q9. Distinct from a Go-live because the Operator and the author are the same person.
- **Go-live** — an Operator taking real money from Buyers on their own Box. Per-operator and repeatable;
  what docs/go-live.md documents. NOT a project-wide event.
- **Public alpha** — this project asserting that a stranger can reach a Go-live unaided. One-way and
  reputational; what lnrent-ea1 / lnrent-2em / lnrent-ehu ultimately serve.
- **Capacity pool** — the physical resource bound of a Box (`box.capacity_json`); always enforced.
- **Recipe cap** — an Operator's optional policy ceiling on how many Instances of one Recipe may be
  live at once. Ceilings, not allocations: caps may sum above the pool.
- **Reservation** — the capacity a pending or active Subscription holds (§9.3). Wire-visible, because
  exhausting it is what a Buyer sees as `capacity_full`.

## Entries that are WRONG or OVERSTATED — do not silently "fix" the wrong one
- **Operator seed (CONTEXT.md:52-59) is WRONG and owned by lnrent-kr1.** It asserts the phoenixd seed
  derivation (`lnrent:phoenixd:v1`) as shipped fact — that string appears in ZERO `.rs` files — and
  claims "One backup covers identity AND the wallet", which docs/go-live.md:21-23 correctly contradicts.
  This is the funds-loss direction: an operator trusting the glossary loses phoenixd funds. Leave the
  FIX to kr1 (its acceptance already requires this entry to be true at close) but ensure whoever closes
  kr1 also reads lnrent-u43: even once the derivation ships, `phoenix.conf` dies with the data dir, so
  the seed alone still does not restore ACCESS.
- **"One Recipe backs many Listings" is OVERSTATED** (CONTEXT.md:94, :99, and the example dialogue at
  :214-218 which narrates publishing two listings from one recipe as if it works). Nothing implements
  it: `listing::d_tag` IS `recipe.service.id` (daemon/src/listing.rs:255-259), which structurally forces
  ONE listing per recipe, and lnrent-ja2 builds a listing PER recipe, not many per recipe.
  SPEC.md:1125-1127's per-size-tier Listings depend on the same missing capability. A glossary may state
  target language, but that example dialogue reads as a description of current behaviour. Add an explicit
  "not yet implemented" note, and file the capability as its own P3 defer rather than leaving it as an
  overpromise.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The six terms above exist in CONTEXT.md, definitions only — no criteria, no procedures.
- The many-Listings-per-Recipe overstatement carries an explicit not-yet-implemented marker, and the
  capability is filed as its own bead.
- The Operator seed entry is left to kr1, with a pointer added here so the coupling is not forgotten.
- Nothing in CONTEXT.md restates a phase list or a gate — those live in the beads and would drift.
